'manners' (mœurs) of antiquity left as 'manners'; style note requires customs.
replacement: When the heroes and customs of antiquity are often brought onto the stage, and playwrights faithfully follow the rules of old precedent, that is enough to conclude that the democratic classes have not yet gained the upper hand in the theaters. In the preface to “Britannicus,” Racine very humbly apologizes for having placed Junia among the Vestals, who, according to Aulus Gellius, he says, “admitted no one below six years of age nor above ten.” We may be sure he would neither have accused himself of this offense nor defended himself against criticism if he had been writing for our contemporaries. A fact of this kind shows the state of literature at the time, and it shows the state of society itself as well. A democratic stage does not prove that the nation is in a state of democracy, because, as we have just seen, even in aristocracies democratic tastes may influence the drama. But when the spirit of aristocracy reigns exclusively on the stage, that fact proves beyond refutation that the whole of society is aristocratic. One may boldly infer that the same lettered and learned class that sways the playwrights also commands the people and governs the country.

Causal connective 'therefore' dropped from 'They therefore content themselves'.
replacement: When the world was managed by a few rich and powerful individuals, these people liked to hold a lofty idea of the duties of man. They were fond of declaring that it is praiseworthy to forget oneself, and that good should be done without hope of reward, as God himself does it. Such were the standard moral opinions of that time. I doubt whether men were more virtuous in aristocratic ages than in others. But they talked ceaselessly about the beauty of virtue, and they studied its usefulness only in private. But now that the imagination takes less lofty flights and every man’s thoughts are centered on himself, moralists are alarmed by this idea of self-sacrifice, and they no longer dare to offer it to the human mind. They therefore content themselves with asking whether the personal advantage of each member of the community does not lie in working for the good of all. When they hit on some point where private interest and public interest meet and merge, they are eager to bring it to notice. Observations of this kind gradually multiply. What was only a single remark becomes a general principle, and it is held to be true that man serves himself in serving his fellow creatures, and that his private interest is to do good.
